label: Get the Job — Learning to Sell
overview: The Get the Job — Learning to Sell content provides a comprehensive advisory sales framework aligned to advisor confidence and client complexity. It contrasts Campaign-based selling (pre-packaged modules for simpler clients) with Total Needs selling (bespoke, exploratory approach for complex, high-value clients). A central Decision Tree guides the advisor to the right path. Six core templates cover the full sales journey — from the first meeting through to negotiation and close. Intermediate-level content suited to senior advisors focused on fee growth. The whole point of the structure is a low-pressure environment: the client always knows what happens next.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Which stage of the sales process are you working on — first meeting preparation, choosing between Campaign and Total Needs approach, running a scoping session, presenting a proposal, or closing and negotiating?

materials.name: Decision Tree & Sales Structure
materials.summary: The strategic brain behind the whole set — a flowchart choosing between Modular/Campaign selling and Bespoke/Total Needs selling based on the client's sophistication and the advisor's own confidence. It removes the guesswork: a new advisor is directed to Free Client Content for a softer experience, a targeted prospect fitting a smaller business profile is routed to Lite Fundamentals. It also makes the approach fit the owner's processing style rather than the advisor's habit.
materials.who_when: Advisors in the planning phase, deciding how to categorise leads and which scoping or presentation pathway will work best. Use it before making contact, not after.
steps: Evaluate the prospect's business profile before any contact, and decide the track: a pre-packaged Campaign for smaller, lower-fee clients, or a bespoke Total Needs process for larger, complex ones.
Weigh your own confidence honestly as well as the client's complexity — the tree exists to match both, not just the client.
If you are new or less confident, start at Free Client Content: it does not end in an offer, so nobody feels channelled and the next conversation stays open.

Identify the prospect's likely processing style and tailor the communication to it — give Reflectors time to withdraw and think, give Pragmatists proof and data, explain the sequence of action to impulsive Activists, and let Theorists contribute their own ideas on the solution.
Use the 8 Pathways map to see the full range of approaches available — Free Client Content, Lite Fundamentals, Specialist Tools and the rest — and pick the one the tree points to.
Note the engagement type you are actually selling — Advice, Facilitation or Education — because it changes how the offer should be framed.

materials.name: Introduction Prompts
materials.summary: A scripted, logical progression for the first meeting, moving from rapport-building into clear expectations, and using an Event, Cause and Effect storytelling model to build credibility without the meeting feeling like an interrogation. It keeps the advisor in control of the conversation through Check Time and Ask Permission scripts. For the owner it lowers anxiety, because the objective is stated and the decision-making process is visible — there is no hidden pitch coming.
materials.who_when: Initial discovery sessions and early-stage prospect meetings where trust and mutual alignment still have to be established.
steps: Open with the Foreplay script to build rapport before any business talk.
Use Check Time to set a professional boundary — agreeing how long you have keeps the meeting yours to run.
State the meeting objective explicitly, so the owner knows exactly what will and will not happen.
Share a relevant Common Problem story using the Event, Cause and Effect model — this builds credibility and empathy without interrogating them.
Ask permission before moving into your approach, so you have the floor to explain it uninterrupted.
Close by confirming whether they are open to a more detailed scoping session, and make the next step explicit.

materials.name: Lite Sales Prompts (SPIDER)
materials.summary: The modular Campaign track, run as a six-step sequence: Show your get-out-of-jail card, Pin the tail on the donkey with the Growth Curve, Investigate blockages, Determine and dangle the prize with the Revenue Model, Ensure the conditions are agreed, and Reveal the golden key. It sets the boundaries — the client's time, their action, the monthly fee — before the solution is revealed. For the owner it puts their struggle in visual context and quantifies what fixing the constraint is actually worth.
materials.who_when: Smaller, less complex business circumstances where a pre-packaged programme is being offered. Typically one to two hours to complete the sale.
steps: Show your get-out-of-jail card — set the terms on which the conversation happens.
Pin the tail on the donkey: place the business on the Growth Curve so they can see where they actually are.
Investigate the blockages holding them at that point.
Determine and dangle the prize using the Revenue Model, so the financial potential of clearing the constraint is a number rather than a hope.
Ensure the three conditions of working together are agreed before anything is revealed — the client commits time, takes action, and agrees to a monthly fee.
Reveal the golden key: the modular programme itself, offered only once the conditions are accepted.

materials.name: Scoping Prompts
materials.summary: The framework for a deep-dive, fact-finding session that explores the internal drivers of the business without the pressure of proposing anything yet. Its discipline is the separation of discovery from solution — the advisor is explicitly not there to solve it in the room. It also gives a structured way to test budget early with a rough range rather than a hard quote, and reassures the client with a privacy statement that this is about challenging their thinking, not filling in a survey.
materials.who_when: Complex engagements and bespoke Total Needs selling, where the nuances of the client's operations must be understood before any proposal exists.
steps: Schedule 1.5 hours — the session needs room, and saying so up front sets the expectation.
Establish at the start that you are there to challenge their thinking, not to provide immediate solutions.
Give the privacy statement, so the client knows where the information goes before they share it.
Guide them through the fact-find, exploring the internal drivers of the business rather than the presenting symptom.
Provide a rough budget estimate at the end — between $x and $y — to qualify the budget without committing to a hard quote.
Confirm the next step and leave the solution for the presentation meeting.

materials.name: Presentation Prompts
materials.summary: The Reveal stage: a structured way to present the offer while systematically neutralising objections. Its central move is Calling out the ghosts — naming and parking the likely concerns, price or delivery, before they can derail the meeting — supported by Trial Closing to test receptiveness as you go. For the owner it takes the emotional charge out of the negotiation: agreeing that neither side has to accept an unworkable deal makes it safe to say what they actually think.
materials.who_when: The pivotal meeting where the tailored solution or formal proposal is presented, leading into the implementation decision.
steps: Set the scene by confirming nothing has changed in the business since you last spoke — a proposal built on stale facts dies in the room.
Call out the ghosts immediately: name the objections you expect, park them openly, and remove the tension before revealing anything.
Reveal the offer, and use trial closing throughout — how does this look, feel, sound? — to test receptiveness rather than waiting for a verdict at the end.
State plainly that neither party has to commit to a deal that does not work, which is what makes the client's honest response safe.
If an unexpected objection surfaces, clarify how important it actually is, state your reply without judgment, and ask how they think both parties could get around it.
Agree the next step before the meeting closes.

materials.name: Implementation Rationale
materials.summary: Manages the final negotiation, and centres on the Emotional Intensity Gap — the distance between what was expected and what is real, which is where negotiations turn sour. It trains the advisor to fix their boundaries in advance by separating must-have from nice-to-have: must have $10,000, would like it paid upfront. Detachment from the outcome is the point, because it is what keeps the advisor objective and lets the client co-solve rather than be argued with.
materials.who_when: Final-stage closing meetings — finalising contracts, defining boundaries, and handling any lingering objections to reach a win-win.
steps: Define your must-have terms and your nice-to-have terms before the meeting, and know your walk-away price.
Manage expectations proactively through the meeting, since the emotional intensity comes from the gap between expectation and reality rather than from the numbers themselves.
Treat every objection as legitimate feedback rather than an argument to win.
When caught by an unexpected objection, scale it objectively — on a scale of 1 to 10, how critical is this? — then invite the client to help solve the difference rather than defending your position.
Hold the boundary: it is perfectly acceptable to decline unprofitable business rather than shoe-horn a deal.
If it is not a fit, excuse yourself tactfully and leave the door open to check back in 6 to 12 months.

advisor_guidance.campaign_vs_total_needs: Campaign selling involves a pre-packaged modular solution — faster, lower fee, suitable for simpler clients. Total Needs selling is explorative and bespoke — more time, higher fee, suited to complex clients with unique problems. Never apply a campaign approach to a complex client, and never over-engineer a simple engagement into a Total Needs process.
advisor_guidance.new_advisor_start: New advisors should start with Free Client Content. This provides a soft sales experience with no forced close — it builds confidence and sets the stage for future paid work without the pressure of a premature pitch.
advisor_guidance.objection_handling: The most effective strategy for objections is to call them out before the client raises them. Name the likely concerns at the start of the Presentation meeting. If an unexpected objection arises late, scale it, state your reply without judgment, and invite the client to co-solve.
